clusters.title: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all | Editorial
clusters.neutral_headline: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up...

items.title: The Guardian view on extreme heat: its scale should be a wake-up call to us all | Editorial
items.standfirst: With thousands dead across Europe this summer, it’s time to recognise heatwaves as the major natural disasters they areThe numbers are now trickling in: nearly 2,900 dead in the UK, at least 35,000 dead across Europe. That’s how many people are believed to have lost their lives in this year’s early-summer heatwaves – the death tolls for the August heatwaves have yet to be counted. In a sense, these people died in a series of natural disasters, similar to the hundreds who died last month after flooding in Nepal, or during the 2024 floods in Valencia, Spain. And yet we do not process these events the same way. Increasingly deadly heatwaves are the most direct and damaging effect of the climate crisis felt in Europe, but they are rarely framed as such.There are some obvious reasons for this. Heatwaves by definition unfold over longer periods than other disasters, they are less dramatic, the majority of those who die are elderly or otherwise vulnerable, and their deaths often take weeks or months to be catalogued and reported, all of which make heatwaves seem less immediate and visible. But while heatwaves will probably never provoke the same visceral shock as earthquakes or tornadoes, it should still be possible to shift the way the public thinks about them, which could save lives and lessen their damage. Continue reading...

items.title: My dad’s determination to choose life despite his cruel illness has taught me gratitude | Nomi Kaltmann
items.standfirst: We can’t control what happens to us – only how we react to it. And when we help others we are reminded that we are more than our sufferingMaking sense of it is a column about spirituality and how it can be used to navigate everyday lifeMy dad, Max, is in his early 60s. More than 15 years ago he was diagnosed with early onset Parkinson’s disease. Since then his illness has progressed, affecting his mobility and making ordinary tasks, like walking, increasingly difficult.My dad is softly spoken and endlessly kind but beneath his gentle exterior is a steely determination. Perhaps this comes from being the son of a sole survivor of the Holocaust. Growing up he was taught that people don’t get to choose the hardships life places before us but we can choose how we react to these challenges.Nomi Kaltmann is an Australian lawyer and journalist. She is a proud member of Melbourne’s Jewish community Continue reading...

clusters.title: Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington
clusters.neutral_headline: Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways...

items.title: Some Americans call us ‘Europoor’ - but there are seven ways we’re exceedingly rich | Emma Beddington
items.standfirst: Our US friends may pity Europeans for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport – but they’re forgetting the really important stuff …I’m sorry to break this to you, but you may be “Europoor”. This is, apparently, what proud American patriots (the kind who describe themselves in those terms on their flag-forward X profiles anyway) are calling us Europeans, mocking us for our low salaries, high taxes and dependence on public transport.GB news presenter Tom Harwood declared this dig “entirely accurate”, but is it? Well, sort of. US post-pandemic GDP growth is more than double that of the eurozone (15.6% compared with 7.2%; the UK is even worse on 6.3%). As for wages, once you adjust for national differences in the cost of essentials such as housing, food and services, the US average is $86,977 compared with the UK’s $66,299, Germany’s $76,286 and France’s $60,483, according to the OECD. A Sunday Telegraph investigation of the “Europoor” question highlighted astronomically powerful growth of the US tech sector supercharged by AI, making it easy to raise and make big money unencumbered by “old world” regulation and taxation. “We don’t want to be like what Europe has become,” said the Republican pollster Brent Buchanan. Continue reading...
